captions: You found a good stock.
Now comes the question nobody teaches — how do
you actually buy it well?
In the next half hour, we'll build one complete
plan: a staggered G T T buy-schedule.
From what a G T T even is, to
the exact price where every order rests. From the
very beginning.
Here's the trap.
You like a stock, so you buy your whole
position today, at today's price.
That's a bet on a single moment.
If it dips the next morning, you feel the
whole fall — and you've got no cash left
to buy cheaper.
A professional does the opposite.

They decide, in advance and in writing, exactly
where
to buy, how much, where to quit, and where
they're aiming.
Then they let orders wait in the market, so
emotion never gets a vote.
That written plan is what we're going to build.
Part one. Order types.
Before the plan, you need the tool.
Let's meet the three kinds of order — and
the one that makes a schedule possible.
Every order answers two questions — what price, and
for how long.
A market order says: buy right now, at whatever
the price is. Fast, but you don't control the
price.
A limit order says: buy only at my price
or better — but it's only valid for today.
If it doesn't fill by the closing bell, it
dies.
Then there's the G T T.
It says: buy at my price — and stay
alive, waiting, for up to one whole year.
That single difference — patience — is what lets
you plan an entry weeks before it happens.
G T T stands for Good Till Triggered.
Think of it as a resting instruction.
You set a trigger price. Then the order just
sits there, dormant, doing nothing.
It watches the last-traded price, tick by tick.
The moment the price touches your trigger, it wakes
up and places your order — automatically.
You don't have to be watching. You don't have
to be awake.

Good till triggered — it waits, patiently, until
your
condition is finally met. That's the whole idea.
So where does this resting order actually sit?
Picture the market as a ladder of prices.
A normal limit order joins a public queue at
the exchange — visible to everyone, and valid only
for today.
A G T T is different. It waits quietly
at your broker, not in the exchange book.
Nobody else sees it.
Only when the price ladder falls to your trigger
does your broker send the real order down to
the exchange.
Until then, it simply rests — one rung on
the ladder, waiting for the market to come to
it.
There are actually two prices in a G T
T.
The trigger price — the level that wakes the
order up.
And the limit price — the price the order
is then placed at.
For a buy, you set the trigger a few
rupees above your limit.
Why? So that when it fires, the price is

already moving through your limit, and the order
actually
fills.
For our first stock, the trigger sits at forty-seven

seventy-five, and the limit just below, at
forty-seven sixty.
A small gap — but it's what makes the
order marketable when it triggers.
G T T comes in two flavours.
The first is Single — one trigger, one order.
That's your entry.
The second is O C O: One Cancels the
Other.
It holds two triggers on the same stock at
once — a target above the price, and a
stop-loss below it.

Whichever one fires first, the other is cancelled
automatically.
So you can bracket a position: if it runs
up, you sell into strength; if it falls, the
stop protects you.
One order, two exits, and you never have to
choose in the heat of the moment.
Part two. The staggered entry.
Now that we have the tool, here's the core
idea of the whole method — and the simple
reason it works.
Let's see the problem clearly.
Buy everything at once, and your average cost is
exactly today's price — one dot on the chart.

Markets don't move in straight lines. Good stocks
still
dip five, eight, ten percent along the way.
If you're all-in at the top, that dip is
pure pain, and you have no cash to answer
it.
But what if you split the buy?
Place part of it lower, and part of it
lower still.
If the dip comes, you buy it — and
your average cost falls. If it doesn't, you still
own a starter position.
You win either way.
So we stagger the entry into two legs, both
resting below today's price.
Leg one is a shallow dip — a normal
pullback, one to three percent down.
Leg two is a deeper dip — a more
serious correction, six to ten percent down.
Each leg is a G T T buy, waiting
at its own price.
For H A L, trading near forty-eight sixty, leg
one rests at forty-seven sixty, leg two down at
forty-five sixty.
Buy some higher, more lower — and your average
lands in between, at forty-six seventy-five.

Lower than where you started, without predicting a
thing.
Part three. Anchoring to the chart.
Those leg prices weren't guesses.
Every number in the plan is pinned to something
real on the chart. Let's see what.
The anchors are moving averages.
A moving average is just the average of the
last N closing prices, drawn as a smooth line
that follows the trend.
Two matter most.

The fifty-day average — the short-term trend. And
the
two-hundred-day average — the long-term trend.
Price tends to fall back toward these lines and
bounce. So they act as support.
For H A L, the fifty-day sits near forty-six
fifty, the two-hundred-day near forty-three eighty.
Leg one hangs at the fifty-day. Leg two reaches

toward the deeper support below. The chart chooses
the
prices, not us.
Now momentum — and this is the R S
I, the Relative Strength Index.
It's a single number from zero to a hundred.
It compares the size of recent gains to recent
losses, over fourteen days. The formula: R S I
equals one hundred, minus one hundred over one plus
average gain divided by average loss.
Above seventy, the stock is overbought — it's run
hot and may pause.
Below thirty, it's oversold — beaten down, and may
bounce.

Between forty-five and sixty-five is a healthy,
sustainable trend.
One crucial thing: R S I does not tell
you direction.
It only tells you whether a move has gone
too far — and that's exactly what helps you
decide whether to chase, or to wait for a
deeper leg.
Let's read R S I on our two names.
H A L sits around fifty-three — right in

the calm, healthy middle. Momentum is fine; there's
no
rush, and no froth.
So buying the first leg near the price is
reasonable.
Syrma is the opposite. Its R S I is
hot, near the top of its range.
That's the market telling you the move is stretched.
Same tool, opposite message — one says you may
step in; the other says wait for a deeper
leg.
R S I doesn't pick the stock. It paces
your entry.
Let's derive the two legs properly, for H A
L.
Start from the price, forty-eight sixty-one.

Leg one: a shallow pullback of one-point-eight
percent, down
to forty-seven sixty — right at the fifty-day line.
That's a normal breather in an uptrend.
Leg two: a deeper dip of nearly six percent,
down to forty-five sixty — the kind of correction
that only comes on a bad week.
Notice: leg one you'll probably get; leg two only
fills if the market really sells off.
That's the point. You're not predicting the dip —
you're ready for it, at a price you decided
calmly.
Every entry needs an exit — two, in fact.
First, the stop-loss.
We place it below leg two, under the two-hundred-day
line, at forty ninety.
It's sized so that from your average of forty-six

seventy-five, the most you can lose is about
thirteen
percent — a bounded, known amount. If the thesis
breaks, the O C O sells automatically.
Second, the target.

The first objective is the fifty-two-week high,
fifty ninety-nine
— about nine percent up.
And to be honest about the dream: a fifty-percent

gain needs seventy twelve; a double needs
ninety-three fifty.
Worth knowing — so the goal stays real.
Now weigh it.
Reward to risk.
For H A L, you're risking about thirteen percent
to your stop, to make about nine percent to
the first target — but because the stop is

far and sized in rupees, the plan's reward-to-risk
works
out near three-point-eight to one.
Good on paper.
But here's the honesty most videos skip.
The valuation says H A L is roughly fairly
priced already.
The bull case is up sixteen percent; the bear
case, down twenty-four.

So that plus-fifty, plus-hundred? That's a bull tail
—
a lovely maybe, not the base case. The growth
is already in the price.
There's an even more honest way to check the
target — imagine three futures.
A bear case, where things disappoint. A base case,
the middle. And a bull case, where everything goes
right.

For each, you multiply a fair price-to-earnings by
the
profit you expect.
Then you weight them by how likely each one
is.
For H A L, that weighted value lands right
around today's price.
The bull case is up sixteen percent; the bear
case, down twenty-four.

So the schedule's reward-to-risk looks great, but
the valuation
says the name is roughly fair.
Both are true. Hold them together.
Last piece — how many shares.
The rule here is one stock a month, with
a budget of thirty to fifty thousand rupees.
You split that budget across the two legs.
For H A L near forty-seven hundred a share,
four shares at leg one and four at leg
two — eight shares in total, an outlay of
about thirty-seven thousand four hundred.
The math has to land on whole shares, so
you round.
A pricey stock like Dixon, at fourteen thousand a
share, might only fit two or three shares —
that's fine. Size to the budget, not to the
ego.
Part four. The plan in action.
Enough theory. Let's run the whole thing end to
end on real names — one clean, one that
tests your discipline.
Watch the full plan fire, on H A L.
The price drifts down.
It touches forty-seven sixty — leg one triggers, and
four shares are bought.
A rough week takes it lower, to forty-five sixty
— leg two triggers, four more shares.

Eight shares now, at an average of forty-six
seventy-five.
Two exits rest in the market: a stop at
forty ninety, a target at fifty ninety-nine.
If it climbs, the target sells and the stop
cancels. If it breaks, the stop sells and the
target cancels.
One plan, placed once — and then you simply
let it work.
Now the hard one — Syrma.

Great little company, but look where it's trading:
right

at its fifty-two-week high, ninety-five percent of
the way
up its yearly range.
Its R S I is hot.
Chase it here, and you're buying the very top.
So the plan demands patience. Leg one waits three
percent down; leg two waits almost ten percent down,
on a real correction.
And here's the discipline: if only leg one fills
and the stock just keeps running, you do not
chase leg two higher.
You let it go, and roll that budget to
next month.
The plan protects you from your own excitement.
A third example, at a very different scale —
Dixon, the electronics maker.

Here one share costs about fourteen thousand six
hundred
rupees.
At a monthly budget of forty thousand, you can
only buy two or three shares — one at
leg one, two at leg two.
That's fine.

And Dixon swings hard. Its beta is over
one-and-a-half,
so it moves faster than the market, both ways.
So the legs sit a little wider, and the
stop, at twelve thousand one hundred, gives it room
to breathe.
Same method — sized and spaced for a wilder,
pricier stock.
Put it together, and you get a schedule —
one pick a month, for five months.
H A L, then Dixon, K E I, Syrma,
and Data Patterns.

A defence anchor, two electronics makers, a cables
compounder,
and a radar specialist.
Each with the same four numbers: two legs, a
stop, and a target — every one anchored to
its own chart.
Spreading the buys across months is itself a stagger
— in time, not just in price.

You're never forced to deploy everything into one
week's
mood.
Finally, placing it — in Kite, conceptually.
You open the stock, choose G T T, and
pick Single for each buy leg — trigger and
limit, quantity, done.
For the exits, you choose O C O, and
set the target above and the stop below in
one order.
Three golden rules.
One — never buy blind; always know your stop
before you enter.
Two — a G T T lasts up to
a year, so review it; prices and stories change.
Three — this is a plan, not a promise.
The market can gap straight through a trigger.
Discipline is the edge — the orders just enforce
it.
Before you go, four ways this plan goes wrong.
One — a gap. If bad news hits, the
price can leap straight past your trigger, and you
fill lower than planned. The plan bounds risk; it
can't erase it.
Two — a stop set too tight. Put it
just under the price, and normal noise will knock
you out. Give it room, below real support.
Three — chasing. The whole point is patience; if
you cancel the wait and buy the top, you've
thrown the plan away.
Four — never reviewing. A G T T lives
for a year; check it, because companies and prices
change.
Avoid these four, and the method does its job.
So — that's the whole staggered G T T
buy-schedule.
A G T T is a patient, resting order.
Single is your entry; O C O brackets the
exit.
You stagger into two legs below the price, anchored

to the fifty and two-hundred-day lines and read
against
R S I.
You bound the loss with a stop, aim at

the fifty-two-week high, and stay honest that a
double
is only the bull case.
Size to your budget, and never chase.
None of this is investment advice — it's a
way of thinking, and a way of removing emotion
from the decision.

Plan the entry, and the exit, before emotion
arrives.
Thanks for watching.
